lesson.title: The Silent H Decoded
lesson.subtitle: hacer ↔ fact, hijo ↔ filial, hierro ↔ ferrous, hambre ↔ famine, hermoso ↔ formosa: seeing Latin F behind Spanish H

hook.title: Seeing the Invisible 'F' Behind Silent 'H'
hook.content: Whenever a native Spanish word starts with H (followed by a single vowel or ie), mentally swap that H for an F and look at the English Latinate cousin: hacer → fac- (manufacture, factory, fact), hijo → fil- (filial, affiliate), hierro → ferr- (ferrous), hambre → fam- (famine), hermoso → form- (formosa, form)!

pattern.title: Everyday vs Learned Doublets Inside Spanish
pattern.content: In fact, Spanish itself often has BOTH the street word in h- and the scholarly word in f-: el hijo ('the son') alongside filial ('filial'), el hierro ('iron') alongside el ferrocarril ('the iron rail = railway')!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: hacer, el hijo, el hierro, el / la hambre, hermoso, hecho
exercises.meaning: to do / to make (manufacture), son / child (filial), iron (ferrous), hunger (famine), beautiful (formosa), done / fact (factum)
exercises.explanation: Every one of these words began with F- in Rome and shifted to silent H- in Castile.

exercises.prompt: Spanish el hijo ('son', hija 'daughter', from Latin fīlius) shares its root with which English adjective meaning 'relating to a son or daughter' (as in '___ piety' or 'affiliate')?
exercises.meaning: filial and affiliate ('to adopt as a son') preserve the Latin f- of hijo!
exercises.explanation: Latin fīlius ('son') gave English filial and affiliate, and Spanish hijo.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'I want to make a reservation' in Spanish?
exercises.meaning: I want to make a reservation
exercises.explanation: hacer covers both 'to do' and 'to make': hacer una reservación.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.meaning: I want to make a reservation today
cues: I want to make: Quiero hacer

summary.outcome: Connect hacer, hijo, hierro, hambre, hermoso, and hecho to their Latin F- cognates.

use_example.german: Mi hijo quiere hacer una reservación en esta ciudad hermosa.
use_example.english: My son wants to make a reservation in this beautiful city.

summary.takeaway: Spanish hacer covers both English 'do' and 'make'.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([2702] The Palatal Twins: -ch- & ll-): master the -ct- → -ch- and pl-/cl- → ll- word families.

twist.prompt: Assemble: 'The iron key (La llave de hierro)'

hacer.context_translation: I want to make a reservation.
hacer.etymology_derivation: Latin facere shifted initial f- to silent h- in Spanish: hacer. English keeps the f in fact and factory.

hijo.etymology_derivation: Latin fīlius gives English 'filial' and Spanish hijo (initial f- silenced to h-).

hierro.shift_rule: Latin ferrum (f- → silent h- AND e → ie)
hierro.etymology_derivation: Look at both shifts firing together: Latin f- became silent h-, and stressed e became ie: ferrum → hierro!

hambre.context_translation: I am very hungry (lit. I have much hunger).
hambre.etymology_derivation: Feminine noun (mucha hambre) that takes el in the singular like el agua, and shows f- → h- from Latin famēs!

hermoso.etymology_derivation: Latin formōsus ('finely formed') — initial f- became silent h-: hermoso!

hecho.english_meaning: done, made (participle of hacer); fact (el hecho)
hecho.shift_rule: Double sound shift: factum → hecho (f→h AND ct→ch!)
hecho.etymology_derivation: Look at Latin factum → Spanish hecho: initial f- became silent h-, AND medial -ct- became -ch-!

reservación.etymology_derivation: Latin reservātiō. Also heard as la reserva in Spain.

tengo.etymology_derivation: Latin teneō developed an epenthetic velar g: tengo.

f_to_h.name: Latin F- ➔ Silent H-
f_to_h.phonetic_rule: Latin initial f- weakened into an aspiration and became completely silent h- in Spanish, while English kept the Latin f- cognate.
f_to_h.historical_linguistics: Castilian contact with Basque/Cantabrian substrate languages lacking initial /f/ caused Latin /f-/ to weaken into silent h-.
f_to_h.philological_note: Hacer ↔ fact/manufacture; hijo ↔ filial; hierro ↔ ferrous; horno ↔ furnace. When you see a silent h-, think f.
